title: Right Side View of a Binary Tree
statement: A binary tree is given to you as a level-order array, where the element at index i is a node's value and index 2*i+1 / 2*i+2 hold its left and right children; null marks a missing node. Imagine standing to the right of the tree and looking at it horizontally: at every depth you can only see the rightmost node that exists at that depth, because it hides everything to its left. Return the list of those visible values, one per depth, ordered from the root's depth downward (top to bottom). Note that the rightmost visible node at a depth may live in a left subtree if the right subtree does not reach that depth. Return an empty list ([]) when the tree is empty.
hints: You need one value per depth, and it is always the last node you would meet if you swept that depth from left to right -- what traversal naturally hands you a whole depth at a time?
Do a breadth-first (level-order) traversal with a queue, processing the tree one full level per iteration; snapshot the queue size at the start of each level so you know where that level ends.

For each level, iterate over exactly the nodes present at the start (size = len(queue)), enqueue every child as you go, and append the value of the final node in that level (index size-1) to your answer; this captures a deep left-subtree node whenever the right subtree stops earlier.
